say.text: Before we build anything, one quick stem.
Which of these is NOT one of the four components of classic TOF?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. ASD and PDA may accompany TOF, but the four components listed by StatPearls and CDC include no ASD, PDA or LVH.
PYQs have keyed PDA, ASD and LVH as "not part of TOF", and current StatPearls lists the same four, so key and source agree here.
Let's rebuild the four from logic, one step at a time, so you never have to memorise them.
Pulmonary stenosis sounds like a valve problem, so 'infundibular' can feel like an extra. But infundibular (sub-pulmonary) RVOT obstruction is itself one of the four.
Look again for a lesion that only sometimes travels with TOF.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this is worth a second look: the infundibular narrowing is a member of the tetrad, not an add-on.

say.text: Hypertrophy sounds like a result rather than a malformation, so it can feel out of place on a list of defects. But right ventricular hypertrophy is the fourth component, secondary to chronic systemic pressures.
Look again for a shunt lesion outside the four.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this is worth a second look: RVH is on the list precisely because it follows from the other changes.

say.text: Say each option as 'a part of one malformed septum and its effects'. Which one fits that description least?
Rung 1: the outflow.
In classic TOF, where does the right ventricular outflow narrowing sit?

choices.label: In the left ventricular outflow tract
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. The component is infundibular (sub-pulmonary) RVOT obstruction.
So the right ventricle now faces a block. Where does its blood go instead?
Pulmonary stenosis sounds like a valve lesion, so the valve is the natural place to look. But the TOF component is named infundibular (sub-pulmonary) RVOT obstruction.
Which level does the name point to?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this is worth a second look: the word 'infundibular' is in the list of four, and 'valve only' is not.

say.text: Outflow obstruction and hypertrophy are familiar on the left side, so it is easy to carry that picture over. But the TOF obstruction is of the right ventricular outflow tract.
Which ventricle does the name point to?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this is worth a second look: the abbreviation is RVOT, with R for right.

say.text: Picture the list of four. Which word describes the obstruction there: valvular, or something else?
Rung 2: the direction of flow.
A narrowed right outflow, a VSD and an overriding aorta. With significant obstruction, where does most of the blood go?

choices.label: Into the lungs, which end up flooded
Toward the aorta, bypassing the lungs
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. With significant RVOT obstruction, most of the blood shunts toward the aorta, bypassing the pulmonary bed.
Less blood reaches the lungs, so a chest film can show decreased pulmonary vascular markings (pulmonary oligaemia).

A VSD usually brings to mind a shunt that floods the lungs, so plethora feels natural. But here the outflow block redirects flow: most of the blood shunts toward the aorta, bypassing the pulmonary bed.
Choose again with the block in mind.
Which of the two exits from the right ventricle is the narrow one now?
Rung 3: cause and effect.
Think of a ventricle pumping against a block, day after day. Which of the four is a consequence of the others rather than a primary malformation?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. RVH is secondary to chronic systemic pressures, so it sits at the end of the chain.
The chain: infundibular obstruction, then the right ventricle works against it, then RVH.
Both sit in the right ventricle, so it is tempting to blame the thick muscle for the narrowing. But the arrow runs the other way: the hypertrophy is secondary to chronic systemic pressures.
Which component follows from the pressure load?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this is worth a second look: the narrowing comes first and the thick muscle follows it.

say.text: If the four sit in your mind as a flat list, any item could be 'secondary'. But only one is described as secondary to chronic systemic pressures: the right ventricular hypertrophy.
Which one is the muscle's response?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this is worth a second look: the overriding aorta is listed as an anatomical alteration, not as a response.

say.text: Ask of each option: is it a shape present from the start, or something that grows over time under strain?
Rung 4: the fifth.
The old term 'pentalogy of Fallot' is TOF plus what?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. Pentalogy of Fallot is TOF plus an atrial septal defect, an old term seldom used now. PYQs expected this and CDC confirms it.
The ASD still sits outside the four; it may accompany TOF.
ASD and PDA both turn up as extra shunts, so they feel interchangeable. But pentalogy is defined as TOF plus an atrial septal defect; a PDA is another anomaly that may accompany TOF.
Which option is the defined fifth?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this is worth a second look: the definition names an atrial septal defect, not a ductus.

say.text: The VSD is the big lesion of TOF, so 'more of the same' feels natural. But pentalogy is TOF plus an atrial septal defect.
Which option fits that wording?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this is worth a second look: the fifth lesion is an ASD, not another VSD.

say.text: Say the options as 'open ductus', 'hole between the upper chambers', 'second ventricular hole'. Which have you seen paired with 'Fallot' in the old term?
Last rung: assemble it.
Which set lists the four components of classic TOF?

choices.label: VSD, overriding aorta, pulmonary stenosis, ASD
VSD, overriding aorta, RVOT obstruction, LVH
VSD, overriding aorta, RVOT obstruction, RVH

say.text: Yes: a large, anteriorly malaligned VSD, an overriding aorta, infundibular RVOT obstruction and RVH.
PYQs have keyed ASD, PDA and LVH as not part of TOF, and StatPearls lists these same four.
ASD is the lesion you just met in the pentalogy, so it is easy to let it into the set. But the four are VSD, overriding aorta, infundibular RVOT obstruction and RVH; ASD may accompany TOF.
Which set has a ventricular change instead?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this is worth a second look: the four include no ASD, PDA or LVH.

say.text: Hypertrophy without a side is easy to store, and left is the familiar side. But the fourth component is right ventricular hypertrophy, secondary to chronic systemic pressures; the list has no LVH.
Which side faces the block?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this is worth a second look: the ventricle that hypertrophies is the one facing the obstruction, the right.

say.text: ASD and PDA are the common 'holes' you know, so a list of shunts feels right. But they may accompany TOF; the four include no ASD or PDA, and do include RVH.
Which set keeps the one-septum story?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this is worth a second look: the four are one VSD, the aorta, the outflow and the ventricle, not a list of shunts.

say.text: Optional depth. Which syndromic association is most common with TOF?
22q11.2 deletion is the most common syndromic association of TOF.
Down syndrome is the best-known syndrome with heart disease, so it is the usual first guess. But the source here names 22q11.2 deletion as the most common syndromic association of TOF.
Turner syndrome is also a familiar heart-disease syndrome, so it comes to mind. But the source here names 22q11.2 deletion as the most common syndromic association of TOF.
How much of TOF carries a 22q11.2 deletion?
Sources differ: up to 15% of TOF cases versus 6% in one TOF cohort. Most common association, not most cases.
'Most common association' can stretch into 'about half'. But sources give up to 15% of TOF cases, or 6% in one cohort.
'Most common association' can stretch into 'nearly all'. But sources give up to 15% of TOF cases, or 6% in one cohort.
A right aortic arch is seen in about what share of TOF?
Yes: a right aortic arch is seen in 20 to 25% of TOF, roughly one in four or five.
Half sounds like a common finding for a named association. But a right aortic arch is seen in 20 to 25% of TOF.
A rare arch variant would be under 1%, which is why it feels plausible. But a right aortic arch is seen in 20 to 25% of TOF.
Two sources quote TOF frequency per 10,000 live births. Which pairing is right?
Yes. Sources differ: 5 to 7 per 10,000 live births in StatPearls, 3–5 in Garagiola and Thorne, and about 3 to 6 in Gagliardi et al.
Similar-sounding ranges swap easily. But StatPearls gives 5 to 7 per 10,000 and Garagiola and Thorne 3–5.
A single round figure is easy to remember. But the sources differ: 5 to 7, 3–5 and about 3 to 6 per 10,000 live births.
